description: "Laplace smoothing and why it is the Bayesian answer to a zero count, the multinomial event model that lets naive Bayes count repeated words, the case for building something quick and dirty first, and the start of support vector machines: functional and geometric margins and the optimisation problem whose solution is the maximum-margin separator."
---

::: {.lecture-video lecture="6"}
:::

*Based on the lecture by Andrew Ng — [CS229](https://cs229.stanford.edu/), Stanford
University, Autumn 2018.*

Naive Bayes, as lecture 5 left it, breaks the first time a word turns up that the
training set never contained: every class gets probability zero and the posterior is
$0/0$. The fix is to add one to every count, and that rule, Laplace smoothing, is
what a Bayesian with a uniform prior would compute anyway. With smoothing in place
the lecture builds a second naive Bayes for text, the multinomial event model, which
counts how often each word occurs instead of only whether it does, and then steps back
to argue that an algorithm this cheap is the right first thing to build. The second
half starts the support vector machine. Before kernels, an SVM is a linear classifier
chosen for one property: of all the lines that separate the training data, it takes
the one that stays furthest from every example. Most of the work is in defining
"furthest" so that it cannot be gamed.

## Laplace smoothing {#sec-laplace}

[4:42]{.t} Ng's example of the zero problem is a word that is new to your inbox but
not to the world. Suppose "NIPS", the machine learning conference, is word 6017 of a
10,000-word vocabulary, and nobody has yet e-mailed you about it. The maximum
likelihood estimates from lecture 5 are fractions of e-mails containing the word, so
both $\phi_{6017 \mid y=1}$ and $\phi_{6017 \mid y=0}$ come out as $0$. [8:03]{.t}
Months later your project team writes about submitting to NIPS. The product
$\prod_j p(x_j \mid y)$ now contains a factor of zero for both classes, and the
classifier's posterior is $0 / (0 + 0)$. The division by zero is the visible symptom;
the underlying error, Ng says, is statistical — estimating the probability of
something as zero because you have not seen it yet.

[9:58]{.t} He sets spam aside to make the point with a smaller example. One season,
Stanford's football team played four out-of-state games — Wake Forest, Oregon State,
Arizona and, Ng adds for the room, Caltech — and lost all four. You followed them to
every one. What is the chance they win the next? Maximum likelihood counts wins over
games played, $0/4 = 0$: absolute certainty of a loss, which is unkind and also
unreasonable. [11:59]{.t} Laplace smoothing pretends you saw one more of each outcome
than you did — one extra win and one extra loss — so the estimate becomes
$(0 + 1)/(4 + 2) = 1/6$.

[12:58]{.t} The rule is not arbitrary. Laplace derived it for the probability that
the sun rises tomorrow: having seen it rise every day so far, you should be very
confident but not certain. Ng compresses the justification into one sentence, which
is worth unpacking. If the unknown win probability $p$ is given a uniform prior on
$[0, 1]$ and you observe $s$ wins in $n$ games, the posterior is proportional to
$p^s (1 - p)^{n - s}$, and its mean is

$$
\mathbb{E}[p \mid \text{data}]
= \frac{\int_0^1 p \cdot p^s (1-p)^{n-s}\, dp}{\int_0^1 p^s (1-p)^{n-s}\, dp}
= \frac{s + 1}{n + 2} .
$$ {#eq-rule-of-succession}

That is exactly the add-one estimate. It is also the posterior predictive probability
that the *next* game is a win, which is the quantity a classifier needs, so "Bayesian
optimal" in the lecture means this: the posterior mean, the best guess under squared
error. The generator integrates the posterior numerically for $0$ wins in $4$ and
recovers $1/6$ to six decimal places, then repeats the check for other counts.

[14:22]{.t} For a variable with $k$ possible values the rule adds one to each count
and $k$ to the denominator,

$$
\hat p(x = j) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^m 1\{x^{(i)} = j\} + 1}{m + k} ,
$$ {#eq-laplace}

which still sums to one over the $k$ values and never returns exactly $0$ or $1$.
[15:14]{.t} For the binary word features of naive Bayes, $k = 2$:

$$
\phi_{j \mid y=1} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^m 1\{x^{(i)}_j = 1,\; y^{(i)} = 1\} + 1}{\sum_{i=1}^m 1\{y^{(i)} = 1\} + 2} ,
$$

and the same for $y = 0$. A word never seen in training now gets a small positive
probability in both classes, the zero factor disappears, and the NIPS e-mail is
classified on the strength of its other words. Ng's assessment of the resulting
filter is measured — "not a great spam classifier but it's not terrible either" —
and its virtue is that training is counting and prediction is multiplying.

## Discretising a continuous feature {#sec-discretising}

[17:58]{.t} Naive Bayes extends past binary features with no change to its structure.
Ng's example goes back to houses, now as a classification problem — will this house
sell within 30 days? — with floor area as a feature. Cut the area into buckets (under
400 square feet, 400 to 800, 800 to 1,200, over 1,200), let $x_j \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$
record which bucket a house falls in, and model $p(x_j \mid y)$ as a multinomial over
four values instead of a Bernoulli over two. The factorisation
$p(x \mid y) = \prod_j p(x_j \mid y)$ is unchanged, the estimates are still counts,
and Laplace smoothing adds $k = 4$ to each denominator. [19:29]{.t} His rule of thumb
when discretising is ten buckets; it "often seems to work well enough", and the board
had room for four.

## The multinomial event model {#sec-event-models}

[20:17]{.t} For text specifically there is a better variant, and Ng motivates it with
what the binary representation throws away. Take the spam e-mail "drugs buy drugs
now", with "buy", "drugs" and "now" at positions 800, 1600 and 6200 of the
vocabulary. [21:40]{.t} Under the representation so far, $x$ is a 10,000-dimensional
binary vector with three ones. The word "drugs" appears twice, and the vector records
it once; the e-mail "drugs buy now" maps to exactly the same $x$
(@fig-event-models). A word that a spammer repeats is arguably stronger evidence than
one that appears once, and the binary model cannot see the difference.

![The e-mail "drugs buy drugs now" under the two event models. Above, one binary entry
per dictionary word; below, one dictionary index per word of the e-mail, so the
repeated word is represented
twice.](../figures/06-support-vector-machines/diagram_event_models.svg){#fig-event-models}

[22:34]{.t} The alternative represents an e-mail of $n$ words as a vector of length
$n$, whose $j$th entry $x_j \in \{1, \dots, 10{,}000\}$ is the dictionary index of
the $j$th word: here $x = (1600, 800, 1600, 6200)$. The length now varies from e-mail
to e-mail, $n_i$ for the $i$th training example, which also answers a property of
text Ng points out — e-mails can be five words long or a thousand, and the binary
representation forces both into one fixed-length vector.

[23:57]{.t} The names are, in Ng's words, "very confusing, very horrible names", but
they are the ones the field uses. The binary model is the *multivariate Bernoulli
event model* — 10,000 coin tosses, one per word, each deciding whether that word
appears. The new one is the *multinomial event model*. [24:49]{.t} Ng credits the
naming to his friend Andrew McCallum, and the paper that compares the two, by
[McCallum and Nigam](https://cdn.aaai.org/Workshops/1998/WS-98-05/WS98-05-007.pdf),
says it set out to clear up exactly this confusion.

[25:12]{.t} The generative story is that the sender first decides spam or not, with
probability $\phi_y$, and then draws each word of the e-mail independently from one
distribution over the vocabulary that depends on the class. So

$$
p(x, y) = p(y) \prod_{j=1}^{n} p(x_j \mid y) ,
$$

which looks identical to lecture 5's naive Bayes and means something different: the
product now runs over the words *of the e-mail* rather than over the dictionary, and
each factor is a multinomial over 10,000 outcomes rather than a coin toss. The
parameters are $\phi_y$ and $\phi_{k \mid y=c} = p(x_j = k \mid y = c)$, the chance
that a word in a class-$c$ e-mail is word $k$. [28:05]{.t} Ng puts a question to the
room — "the chance of word blank being blank" — and the answer, *any* position being
word $k$, exposes the hidden assumption: the distribution does not depend on $j$. The
first word of a spam e-mail is "drugs" with the same probability as the third, which
is why $j$ does not appear on the left-hand side.

[29:41]{.t} The maximum likelihood estimates are again counts, now over word
occurrences instead of e-mails, and with Laplace smoothing they are

$$
\phi_{k \mid y=0} =
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} 1\{x^{(i)}_j = k,\; y^{(i)} = 0\} + 1}
     {\sum_{i=1}^m 1\{y^{(i)} = 0\}\, n_i + 10{,}000} .
$$ {#eq-multinomial-mle}

In English: pool every word of every non-spam e-mail, and ask what fraction of them
are word $k$. If the non-spam e-mails contain 100,000 words in all and "drugs" is 200
of them, the unsmoothed estimate is $200/100{,}000$. [31:59]{.t} Ng asks the room what
to add to the denominator for smoothing, and the answer is the number of values $x_j$
can take: the vocabulary size, 10,000, not two.

[33:44]{.t} A student asks what to do with a word that is not in the dictionary at
all. Either drop it, or map every out-of-vocabulary word to one special token,
conventionally `UNK`, which then gets a probability like any other word. The second
keeps the information that the e-mail contained rare words, which can itself be
evidence.

The multinomial model is still a linear classifier, now in word *counts*. Taking the
log of Bayes' rule, the log-odds of spam is

$$
\log \frac{p(y=1 \mid x)}{p(y=0 \mid x)}
= \log \frac{\phi_y}{1 - \phi_y} + \sum_{k=1}^{10{,}000} c_k \log \frac{\phi_{k \mid y=1}}{\phi_{k \mid y=0}} ,
$$

where $c_k$ is the number of times word $k$ occurs in the e-mail. The generator
confirms this against Bayes' rule on 200 random e-mails. A repeated word now adds its
weight once per occurrence, which is precisely the information the Bernoulli model
discarded. McCallum and Nigam's comparison on five corpora found the Bernoulli model
competitive with small vocabularies and the multinomial model usually better with
large ones, averaging a 27 percent reduction in error — "much better", as the lecture
puts it, for the typical text problem.

::: {.callout-note title="In the official notes"}
cs229-notes2, section 2.1, gives Laplace smoothing for the binary naive Bayes model;
section 2.2 writes out the multinomial event model's likelihood and both smoothed
estimates.
:::

## Build something quick and dirty first {#sec-quick-and-dirty}

[35:26]{.t} Naive Bayes is rarely the most accurate choice — logistic regression
usually beats it — so the question is what it is for. Ng's answer is a piece of
working advice that appears in no PDF. [36:55]{.t} If your goal is to make a learning
algorithm work for an application, rather than to invent a new algorithm, start by
implementing something simple and fast, train it, look at how it fails, and let the
failures decide what to build next. [38:11]{.t} His analogy is software: nobody
writes 10,000 lines of code and compiles them for the first time at the end; you
write a module, test it, and build up. A complicated learning system designed in full
before any of it runs is the same mistake.

[39:07]{.t} The spam filter shows why. Ng started a conference on e-mail and anti-spam,
and his example list of promising ideas is long. Spammers misspell deliberately —
"m0rtgage", or the word broken up with slashes — so a filter keyed to words sees an
unknown token where a person sees "mortgage"; one of his students published on mapping
such spellings back to words. Spammers spoof headers to hide where mail came from.
You could fetch the URLs in an e-mail and analyse the pages behind them. [40:59]{.t}
Each of these is three to six months of work, and at the start you cannot know which
one matters. So build the crude filter, then read the e-mails it gets wrong. If many
of them are deliberate misspellings, you now have evidence that the misspelling
problem is worth months; if few are, "don't bother" — and you have saved the months.
This is error analysis, which the course returns to later.

[42:06]{.t} That is the niche for naive Bayes and GDA. Neither will give the best
accuracy; logistic regression, SVMs and neural networks almost always do better. But
both are non-iterative — counting, or computing means and covariances — and short to
write, so they are a fast way to get the first system running. Ng's advice for course
projects follows: do not spend weeks designing; get a data set and apply something
simple, logistic regression or naive Bayes rather than a neural network, and go from
there.

[44:26]{.t} A student points to a weakness of the word features themselves: "mother"
and "father", or "one" and "two", are entirely unrelated indices to naive Bayes, which
has no way to know that similar words should behave similarly. Ng agrees and names the
fix from neural networks, *word embeddings*, which represent each word by a vector
learned so that related words land close together. Because the embedding comes with
that knowledge built in, a classifier built on it needs fewer labelled examples. The
course leaves the topic to CS230 and CS224N.

## Why support vector machines {#sec-why-svm}

[46:22]{.t} The SVM enters with a picture: two classes in the plane whose boundary is
clearly curved. Logistic regression and GDA, as they stand, draw straight lines.
[47:06]{.t} You can get a curve out of logistic regression by inventing features —
map $(x_1, x_2)$ to $\phi(x) = (x_1, x_2, x_1^2, x_2^2, x_1 x_2, x_1^3, \dots)$ and
fit the same linear model to $\phi(x)$ — and with the quadratic terms the boundary
can become an ellipse (@fig-quad-boundary). The generator fits both models to the
same data: on the raw features logistic regression misclassifies a third of the
training set, with the quadratic terms 12 percent.

![Logistic regression on the same data with and without hand-picked features. With
$x_1, x_2$ alone the boundary must be a straight line and it gives up; with the
squares and the product added, the boundary is an ellipse around the inner
class.](../figures/06-support-vector-machines/diagram_quad_boundary.svg){#fig-quad-boundary}

[48:05]{.t} The trouble is choosing the features. An ellipse needs quadratic terms;
Ng admits he would not know which features produce the irregular boundary he drew,
and nobody wants to guess between $\sqrt{x_1}$ and $(x_1 x_2)^{2/3}$. The SVM's
promise is to map $x$ into a much higher-dimensional feature space — [51:15]{.t}
hundreds of thousands of dimensions, or infinitely many — and fit a linear classifier
there, which is non-linear back in the original space, without anyone choosing the
features by hand. That is the *kernel* idea of lecture 7.

[48:48]{.t} Ng's other reason is practical. The SVM is "turnkey": mature software
solves its optimisation problem reliably, without a learning rate to tune or a
convergence to babysit. He is explicit that for many problems neural networks are now
more effective, and equally explicit that practice uses a much wider set of tools than
the press coverage of deep learning suggests.

[49:57]{.t} The road map has three stages: the *optimal margin classifier* for data
that a straight line can separate, which this lecture starts; kernels, which run it in
huge feature spaces; and a modification for data that cannot be separated. The first
stage needs two definitions of margin.

## The functional margin {#sec-functional-margin}

[54:50]{.t} Ng motivates the margin with logistic regression. The classifier predicts
$1$ when $\theta^\top x \ge 0$, but a correct prediction can be confident or marginal.
If $y^{(i)} = 1$ we would like $\theta^\top x^{(i)} \gg 0$, so that
$g(\theta^\top x^{(i)})$ is close to $1$; if $y^{(i)} = 0$ we would like
$\theta^\top x^{(i)} \ll 0$. A classifier for which both hold on every example is
correct and confident.

[1:00:02]{.t} The SVM changes notation to make the algebra cleaner. Labels are
$y \in \{-1, +1\}$, the hypothesis outputs a hard $\pm 1$ instead of a probability,
$g(z) = 1$ if $z \ge 0$ and $-1$ otherwise, and the intercept is pulled out of the
parameter vector: $h_{w,b}(x) = g(w^\top x + b)$, with $b$ playing the role of
$\theta_0$ and $w$ of $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_n$, and no $x_0 = 1$ convention.

[1:03:36]{.t} The *functional margin* of the hyperplane $(w, b)$ with respect to the
example $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ is

$$
\hat\gamma^{(i)} = y^{(i)} \left( w^\top x^{(i)} + b \right) .
$$ {#eq-functional-margin}

The label folds the two hopes into one: if $y^{(i)} = 1$ we want $w^\top x^{(i)} + b$
large and positive, if $y^{(i)} = -1$ large and negative, and either way we want
$\hat\gamma^{(i)}$ large. [1:06:30]{.t} Its sign alone already says something:
$\hat\gamma^{(i)} > 0$ exactly when the example is classified correctly.
[1:07:46]{.t} For the whole training set, the SVM takes the worst case,
$\hat\gamma = \min_i \hat\gamma^{(i)}$ — how well the classifier does on the example
it does worst on. That is a harsh notion, and it makes sense for now only because
this lecture assumes the data are linearly separable.

[1:09:01]{.t} The functional margin has a flaw Ng calls cheating. Multiply $w$ and
$b$ by $2$, or $10$, and every $\hat\gamma^{(i)}$ multiplies by the same factor, yet
the boundary $w^\top x + b = 0$ is the same line and every prediction is unchanged
(the generator checks this for factors of $2$, $10$ and $1/17$, Ng's choices). So
"make the functional margin large" is not a goal at all: any separating classifier
achieves an arbitrarily large one. [1:10:00]{.t} The fix is to normalise — require
$\lVert w \rVert = 1$, or equivalently divide $w$ and $b$ by $\lVert w \rVert$ — and
the freedom to rescale $(w, b)$ without changing the classifier turns out to be
useful later rather than only a nuisance.

## The geometric margin {#sec-geometric-margin}

[1:11:29]{.t} The geometric margin is the normalised version, and it has a picture.
The line $w^\top x + b = 0$ splits the plane into the half where the classifier
predicts $+1$ and the half where it predicts $-1$, and the vector $w$ is perpendicular
to the line, pointing into the positive half. [1:12:33]{.t} For a correctly classified
positive example $A$, the *geometric margin* $\gamma^{(i)}$ is its Euclidean distance
to the line: the length of the segment from $A$ to the nearest point $B$ on the
boundary (@fig-margins).

![The geometric margin of one example. The boundary is $w^\top x + b = 0$ with
$w = (2, 1)$ and $b = -2$; $w$ is perpendicular to it; the positive example $A$ sits
at distance $\gamma^{(i)}$ from its foot $B$ on the
line.](../figures/06-support-vector-machines/diagram_margins.svg){#fig-margins}

[1:13:49]{.t} Ng states the formula and leaves the derivation to the notes; it is
short enough to give. $B$ is $A$ moved back along the unit normal by the distance
$\gamma^{(i)}$, so $B = x^{(i)} - \gamma^{(i)} w / \lVert w \rVert$, and $B$ lies on
the line, so $w^\top B + b = 0$. Solving gives
$\gamma^{(i)} = (w^\top x^{(i)} + b)/\lVert w \rVert$ for a positive example, and
including the label makes it hold for negative ones too:

$$
\gamma^{(i)} = y^{(i)} \left( \frac{w^\top x^{(i)} + b}{\lVert w \rVert} \right)
= \frac{\hat\gamma^{(i)}}{\lVert w \rVert} .
$$ {#eq-geometric-margin}

For the point $A = (2, 1.6)$ in @fig-margins, the functional margin is $3.6$ and the
geometric margin $3.6 / \sqrt 5 \approx 1.61$; multiply $w$ and $b$ by ten and the
functional margin becomes $36$ while the geometric margin stays at $1.61$. The
geometric margin is the functional margin with the cheat removed. The generator
checks @eq-geometric-margin against an explicit projection onto the hyperplane for
500 random hyperplanes and points in three dimensions. [1:15:23]{.t} As before, the
training set's geometric margin is the worst case, $\gamma = \min_i \gamma^{(i)}$.

## The optimal margin classifier {#sec-optimal-margin}

[58:15]{.t} Ng drew the motivating picture well before the definitions. Two lines
both separate a training set perfectly; one passes close to a few of the examples, the
other keeps a wide berth from both classes, and the second "looks much better". The
geometric margin is what "looks better" means: the first line's worst example is
barely on the right side, the second line's is far from it (@fig-optimal-margin).

![Two lines that both separate the training set. The dotted one passes within $0.10$
of the closest example; the solid one, the maximum-margin separator, keeps a
geometric margin of $0.77$ from both classes. The dashed lines are where
$w^\top x + b = \pm 1$, and the circled examples on them are the support
vectors.](../figures/06-support-vector-machines/diagram_optimal_margin.svg){#fig-optimal-margin}

[1:16:28]{.t} The *optimal margin classifier* chooses $w$ and $b$ to maximise the
geometric margin of the training set. [1:17:59]{.t} Ng poses it as a problem in three
unknowns, $\gamma$, $w$ and $b$:

$$
\max_{\gamma, w, b} \; \gamma
\quad \text{subject to} \quad
\frac{y^{(i)} (w^\top x^{(i)} + b)}{\lVert w \rVert} \ge \gamma ,
\quad i = 1, \dots, m .
$$ {#eq-max-margin}

Every example must have geometric margin at least $\gamma$, and $\gamma$ is pushed
as high as the constraints allow, so at the optimum $\gamma$ equals the worst
example's margin and that worst margin is as large as it can be.

[1:19:03]{.t} In this form the problem is not convex, so there is no guarantee that a
local method finds the global optimum. [1:19:13]{.t} Ng states, and leaves the steps
to lecture 7 and the notes, that a few rewrites turn it into an equivalent convex
problem: minimise $\frac12 \lVert w \rVert^2$ subject to every functional margin
being at least $1$. His one-line intuition is that the margin is the functional
margin divided by $\lVert w \rVert$, so a smaller $w$ means a smaller divisor and a
larger geometric margin. Off-the-shelf solvers handle the convex form, and for
separable data its solution is the optimal margin classifier — "really a baby SVM",
which kernels will grow up.

The solution has a property the picture already shows. In @fig-optimal-margin only
two examples touch the dashed lines; they are the *support vectors*, and the
separator depends on them alone. The generator finds this separator in two
independent ways. It searches over directions for the one that leaves the widest gap
between the classes, and then checks the result against the optimality conditions of
the convex problem: every functional margin is at least $1$, the two closest examples
have functional margin exactly $1$, and $w = \sum_i \alpha_i y^{(i)} x^{(i)}$ over those
two examples alone, with both $\alpha_i > 0$. That last fact — the solution is built from a
few training examples — is where lecture 7 begins.

::: {.callout-note title="In the official notes"}
cs229-notes3, sections 1–4, defines the functional and geometric margins with the
same notation and gives the full chain of rewrites from @eq-max-margin to the convex
quadratic program.
:::
